0.long_answer: Baruch Samuel Blumberg’s Nobel-winning work led to the identification of the hepatitis B virus (HBV), first recognized through the "Australia antigen." HBV is a small, enveloped, partially double-stranded DNA virus that is taxonomically classified in the family Hepadnaviridae; thus, Hepadnaviridae is the virus family that includes the infectious agent he discovered.

Perimyositis is defined as inflammation of the perimysium—the connective tissue sheath that surrounds muscle fascicles. Inflammation is the canonical biological response of vascularized connective tissue to harmful stimuli (e.g., pathogens, toxins, trauma). Therefore, perimyositis represents exactly such an inflammatory response occurring in the connective tissue around muscle, confirming that it is indeed part of that biological process.

Loss-of-function mutations in the ALDH18A1 gene, which encodes Δ¹-pyrroline-5-carboxylate synthase (P5CS), cause the autosomal-recessive cutis laxa type IIA/De Barsy progeroid syndrome. Affected patients show premature-aged (progeroid) appearance with lax, wrinkled skin (cutis laxa), growth and developmental delay, and characteristic ocular manifestations such as corneal clouding, confirming ALDH18A1 deficiency as the molecular basis of the syndrome.
Cuffer and Barbillon used a stethoscope to hear the mid-systolic click in 1887. The stethoscope was first devised by René Laennec in 1816, making 1816 the year of the instrument’s invention.

In laryngeal (recurrent respiratory) papillomatosis, human papillomavirus infects the squamous mucosa at the squamo-columnar junction of the larynx. Papillomatous growths most often arise on the true vocal cords (vocal folds), the commonest laryngeal site for these benign tumors before they may spread to other laryngeal surfaces.

All six reported cases of keratosis follicularis-dwarfism-cerebral atrophy syndrome have been described in children from Panama. Panama proclaimed its independence from the Spanish Empire on 28 November 1821, making 1821 the year in question.

Doxycycline is a broad-spectrum tetracycline antibiotic routinely prescribed to treat Chlamydia trachomatis infection, often dubbed the “silent epidemic” because it is frequently asymptomatic. The same drug is also recommended by health authorities such as the CDC and WHO for chemoprophylaxis against Plasmodium falciparum malaria, making it a dual-use agent for both chlamydia therapy and malaria prevention.

Yes. Multiple benign pigmented lesions—termed eruptive melanocytic nevi—have been reported to appear during the re-epithelialisation phase after toxic epidermal necrolysis. The massive epidermal loss in TEN is followed by rapid melanocyte proliferation and redistribution, and several case reports document the sudden development of numerous small benign nevi on previously affected skin. Thus, eruptive melanocytic nevi constitute a recognised, though uncommon, cutaneous complication of TEN.

Mevalonate kinase deficiency (hyper-IgD syndrome) is an autoinflammatory disorder that presents with recurrent, unexplained febrile episodes. Because these fevers lack an obvious infectious, malignant, or autoimmune cause, patients with MKD often meet the clinical definition of fever of unknown origin (FUO). Consequently, FUO is routinely included in the differential diagnosis of MKD in clinical practice and in authoritative reviews of autoinflammatory diseases.

Abruzzo-Erikson syndrome is an early synonym for CHARGE syndrome, and CHARGE syndrome is caused in most patients by pathogenic variants in the CHD7 gene. Thus, the syndrome is definitively linked to CHD7 mutation.

The oriental rat flea, Xenopsylla cheopis, is the principal vector that transmits the plague bacterium Yersinia pestis from infected rodents to humans. Its feeding behavior and high efficiency in developing a blocked proventriculus that regurgitates bacteria into the bite site make it the primary species responsible for human plague outbreaks worldwide.

Protocadherin-7 (PCDH7) is a non-clustered member of the protocadherin subfamily within the cadherin superfamily. Rare deletions and pathogenic variants involving PCDH7 have been detected in patients with congenital esophageal atresia/tracheoesophageal fistula, and its role in cell-adhesion during foregut development supports its designation as a candidate gene for this malformation.

Neurocysticercosis, the infection of the central nervous system by the larval stage of the pork tapeworm Taenia solium, is reported to involve the brain in about 10–24 % of documented cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) cases. The inflammatory reaction to cysticerci in the subarachnoid space and venous walls promotes endothelial injury and hypercoagulability, predisposing to thrombosis of the dural venous sinuses and thus linking this parasitic disease to CVST.

A median sternotomy is the standard cardiac surgical approach in which the surgeon makes a single vertical mid-line incision through the skin and splits the sternum to open the anterior mediastinum, providing wide access to the heart, great vessels and lungs. Because the skin incision runs straight down the centre of the chest, postoperative healing can lead to prominent, sometimes keloid, scarring over the sternum.

Shprintzen–Goldberg syndrome (SGS) is a rare congenital multiple-anomaly disorder produced by heterozygous pathogenic variants in the SKI gene located on chromosome 1p36. Patients show craniosynostosis, marfanoid habitus, and pronounced arachnodactyly—very long, slender 'spider fingers'—among other skeletal and connective-tissue features.

Mutations in the VPS33B gene cause arthrogryposis–renal dysfunction–cholestasis (ARC) syndrome. VPS33B encodes a Sec1/Munc18-like protein that is a core component of the HOPS/CORVET tethering machinery. Its principal role is to mediate vesicle-mediated protein sorting, controlling the tethering and fusion of intracellular transport vesicles essential for proper apical–basolateral polarity and lysosomal trafficking. Loss of this vesicle-sorting function underlies the multisystem defects seen in ARC syndrome.

Naproxen is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug widely prescribed for chronic inflammatory disorders, including rheumatoid arthritis. Clinical and public-health guidelines for Chikungunya management (e.g., CDC/WHO) list naproxen as an appropriate NSAID to reduce the fever, arthralgia, and joint swelling characteristic of acute Chikungunya infection.

The first genetic change shown to cause Moyamoya disease type 2 was the missense variant p.Arg4810Lys (c.14429G>A; often reported as p.R4859K) in the RNF213 gene on chromosome 17q25.3. This substitution was identified in Japanese families in which it co-segregated with the autosomal-dominant form of the disease and was subsequently confirmed as the major susceptibility allele for Moyamoya in East-Asian populations, establishing RNF213 as the MMD2 gene.

The eyelid drooping (ptosis) observed in Joubert syndrome results from weakness or dysfunction of the levator palpebrae superioris muscle, the main skeletal muscle responsible for elevating the upper eyelid; impaired action of this muscle leads directly to the characteristic eyelid ptosis seen in affected individuals.

Deferiprone—an oral iron-chelating agent—was authorised by the European Medicines Agency in 1999 and received U.S. FDA approval 12 years later (2011) for patients with transfusional iron overload in thalassemia major when other chelators are inadequate. Because it binds excess ferric iron, the same mechanism is leveraged to reduce systemic iron in hereditary hemochromatosis, making deferiprone a therapy for both conditions.

Ayazi syndrome is described primarily by X-linked intellectual disability with additional features such as short stature, distinctive craniofacial characteristics, and sometimes hearing loss. The clinical literature and rare-disease databases do not list obesity (excessive body fat with potential health harm) among its core or reported manifestations. Therefore, excessive body fat is not considered a symptom of Ayazi syndrome.

Early myoclonic encephalopathy (EME) is a rare, severe epileptic encephalopathy that begins in the neonatal period or within the first three months of life. It is typified clinically by fragmentary or erratic myoclonic jerks and, at times, violent myoclonic spasms. EEG shows a characteristic suppression-burst pattern, and the condition carries a very poor prognosis, distinguishing it as one of the most malignant early-onset epilepsies.

Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome confers a markedly elevated risk of developing childhood cancers—especially Wilms tumor, hepatoblastoma, neuroblastoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma. Malignant neoplasms are the second leading cause of death in U.S. children aged 1–14 years (after unintentional injuries). Because BWS increases the incidence of these cancers by roughly 10- to 20-fold compared with the general pediatric population, the syndrome does indeed raise the risk of this major cause of childhood mortality.

The physician who holds the Cullen Endowed Chair at Baylor College of Medicine is James R. Lupski. Together with Dr. Lorraine Potocki, Dr. Lupski published the seminal description of the 17p11.2 microduplication that now bears their names—Potocki-Lupski syndrome—in the first detailed clinical and molecular report. Thus, saying that he was among the first to describe the syndrome is accurate, so the statement is not incorrect.

Yes. Juvenile ankylosing spondylitis belongs to the HLA-B27–associated spondyloarthritides, which characteristically lack autoantibodies directed against nuclear antigens. Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) are therefore typically absent or only rarely detected, in contrast to diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus or the oligoarticular form of juvenile idiopathic arthritis where ANA positivity is common.

The hepatitis B surface antigen (the “Australia antigen”) was first isolated and characterised by Baruch Samuel Blumberg, work that earned him the 1976 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. The physician who married Veronica Tester was a different individual, therefore the two roles were not held by the same person.

Thiamine (vitamin B1) is routinely given to patients undergoing alcohol withdrawal because chronic alcohol use depletes thiamine stores and impairs its absorption. Thiamine is an essential co-factor for cerebral glucose metabolism; deficiency precipitates Wernicke encephalopathy, characterized by ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and confusion. Administering thiamine before or with glucose replenishes stores and effectively prevents this neurological complication.

Electrosurgery (radiofrequency electrodessication/fulguration) is documented in dermatologic guidelines and case reports as an accepted destructive option for localized or hypertrophic lesions of Darier disease—the autosomal dominant keratinization disorder produced by ATP2A2 mutations. Although not first-line therapy (systemic or topical retinoids are), electrosurgical removal of abnormal keratotic growths is a recognized, clinically used treatment modality for this condition.

The triad of gait instability, cognitive decline, and urinary urgency/incontinence typifies normal-pressure hydrocephalus. Definitive first-line therapy is surgical diversion of cerebrospinal fluid by placing a ventriculoperitoneal shunt, which lowers ventricular pressure and typically improves gait and bladder function most markedly.

Grover disease, also called transient acantholytic dermatosis, was first described in 1975 by the American dermatopathologist Dr. Ralph W. Grover. On skin biopsy it shows focal acantholysis—the loss of intercellular desmosomal connections—exactly the histologic change characteristic of pemphigus vulgaris and notably absent in bullous pemphigoid, which instead produces a subepidermal split without acantholysis.

The clinician–scientist who first defined Hereditary Non-polyposis Colorectal Cancer Syndrome, Dr. Henry T. Lynch, was honored by the American Cancer Society in 1992 (receiving its Distinguished Service/Clinical Research Professor award). Therefore, the answer is affirmative.

Among the disorders considered when evaluating patients with loin pain hematuria syndrome is systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), because lupus nephritis can present with flank pain and hematuria.  The complement C1q gene cluster (C1QA, C1QB, C1QC) that confers strong genetic susceptibility to SLE is located at chromosome cytoband 1p36.12, linking SLE with this specific cytogenetic region.

In some patients, varicella-zoster virus spreads to the brain parenchyma, causing varicella encephalitis. The resulting inflammation produces focal neurological deficits; typical clinical signs include dizziness or ataxia, dysarthria, unilateral weakness (hemiparesis), and sensory disturbances like paresthesia, making encephalitis one of the most serious complications of primary VZV infection.

Skeletal muscle fibres are multinucleated cells built from repeating sarcomeres, and they rely heavily on anaerobic glycolysis. The predominant lactate dehydrogenase isoenzyme in such tissue is LDH-5, composed of four muscle (M) subunits (M4). This isoform efficiently converts pyruvate to lactate under the low-oxygen conditions typical of contracting skeletal muscle.

Lymph nodes are small bean- or kidney-shaped immune organs located along lymphatic vessels. In pancreatic cancer, involvement of regional lymph nodes (peripancreatic, celiac, superior mesenteric, para-aortic, etc.) constitutes the N component of the TNM staging system. Determining whether these lymph nodes harbor metastatic tumor cells is therefore critical for accurate staging, prognosis, and treatment planning in patients with pancreatic cancer.

The scientist who performed the first successful chorionic villus sampling was the Ukrainian-born biologist Yury Verlinsky. Before developing this early-pregnancy prenatal diagnostic technique, Verlinsky completed his undergraduate studies in Biology at Kharkiv State University (now V. N. Karazin Kharkiv National University) in Ukraine.

Cartilage–Hair Hypoplasia is frequently accompanied by cellular immunodeficiency with marked lymphopenia; adult patients commonly have absolute lymphocyte counts well below the normal lower limit (≈1.5 × 10⁹/L). A value under 0.9 × 10⁹/L therefore falls into the range reported for CHH-associated T-cell deficiency, making the diagnosis plausible and warranting further evaluation.

Psychogenic purpura, also called Gardner-Diamond syndrome or autoerythrocyte-sensitization syndrome, is an exceptionally rare bleeding disorder characterized by spontaneous, painful ecchymoses. Epidemiologic reviews show a striking female predominance—women comprise roughly 85-90 % of reported cases—making it the subtype of purpura that fits the description in the question.

The most prevalent arthritis is osteoarthritis, a non-inflammatory joint disease. Synovial fluid aspirated from osteoarthritic joints is typically non-turbid, highly viscous, and exhibits the characteristic pale-yellow (“straw-colored”) tint seen in normal or non-inflammatory joint fluid.

Hodgkin lymphoma represents roughly 10 % of all lymphoma diagnoses worldwide. Epidemiologic and molecular studies show that latent Epstein-Barr virus genomes are present in about 40–50 % of Hodgkin lymphoma tumors, demonstrating a frequent association between this virus and the disease.
